newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-WIN says will be on time and affordable.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-WIN says will be on time and affordable.

text.p: An electronic communications system being developed for the insurance industry will be launched next year at a price that even small operators can afford and with potential for 300,000-500,000 users, its joint chief executive David Evans told Reuters.

Evans confirmed that the World Insurance Network (WIN), the much-vaunted system announced a year ago but so far unseen, was now under testing and would be ready for unveiling at a London technology conference on February 19.

"We have been cautious. We are here to develop a quality product. We've produced a business plan which is fully funded and there are products to bring to market. This is not a case of smoke and mirrors," Evans said.
Evans said WIN had been cautious about setting deadlines and unveiling prototypes of the system.
"We are also wary of showing products too soon which affect people's futures."
However, WIN does not have the field to itself and other systems are in development, particularly on the internet.

One newcomer is the London Market Intranet, backed by NetSoft Solutions Limited, which already provides services to London Market insurers. It uses industry standard protocols and off-the-shelf products.

WIN also wants to avoid the problems encountered by the Electronic Placing Support (EPS) system introduced to the London insurance market in 1992 with a roll-out schedule that proved impossible to meet.
Against this background, WIN has chosen to avoid setting deadlines and targets and shied away from the glare of publicity until it can be sure it has a tried and tested product.
"We are very carefully feeling out what we and our trading partners want to do. We don't want to start committing ourselves until we know what we can do,"Evans said.

WIN is being developed by the world's six biggest insurance brokers -- Alexander & Alexander, Aon Corp, Johnson & Higgins, Marsh & McLennan, Sedgwick Group Plc and Willis Corroon Group Plc. It is based in the UK and plans a U.s. office in January. British Telecommunications and MCI are providing communications expertise.

A group of five insurers is involved in the development, but they wish to remain anonymous until the unveiling. Evans also said he had recently received encouragement from a group of Swiss insurance firms.

"We deliberately limited the initial development stage of WIN to six rather than inviting a cast of thousands," Evans said, adding that this gave the project sufficient backing while not making it too cumbersome.

Evans said the pricing structure was being finalised after surveys to see what the market will bear. The outline is for a membership fee plus an annual subscription. There will be an element of pay-as-you-go, plus bolt-on added value services such as online news and information for an extra fee.

The entry cost for small firms will be low as it is intended that the service will be open to everyone in the insurance industry once it is up and running, Evans said, adding that because WIN is personal computer based, it will not involve large hardware expenditure by users.
"The aim is that it will be integrated and affordable. It should drive services up and costs down," he said.

He added that the brokers supporting the scheme will pay the same rates as everyone else. He also confirmed that the big six would not jointly insist that their staffs use the system or that they would set joint usage quotas, although he added that "the preferred way of working will be on WIN".
WIN should go live in the first half of 1997, Evens said, initially with a secure messaging and e-mail service and a global insurance directory for members over an Intranet system called WinConnect.
Subsequent planned developments include document scanning, online information services and video conferencing.

The insurance industry's experience of introducing electronic systems has been mixed. Some are widely used, particularly in back office claims handling and settlement, but other initiatives have proved less successful and none can claim to be global market leaders.
"The challenges aren't just technical, this is a cultural issue," Evans said, noting that it was important that WIN should be a product that people in the industry want to use.
Evans declined to say how much had been invested in WIN so far, but said the backers intended to cover their costs and fund future development rather than make money out of running the system.
"The six founders are in this to take costs out of the industry. It's an enabling mechanism, not an alternative income stream."
-- Reuters Insurance News 44 171 542 2769
